activities.anchor: iron sticks to magnets, copper doesn't
activities.caption: file each fact under its magnetic class
activities.name: ssMagSort

config.prompt: Magnetism in matter — file each fact:

items.label: iron, cobalt, nickel — neighbouring spins align cooperatively into domains
hammering or heating can demagnetise it — domain-realigning
the fridge magnet, engineered with fine particles to hold its domains
unpaired spins align weakly with a field
what iron becomes above its 770 °C Curie temperature

config.why: Ferromagnetism is a collective phase, not a per-atom property — the same lattice, the same atoms, and above the Curie point the magnetism is simply gone.

activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's scrap-yard notes
activities.name: ssScrapSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's scrap-yard notes is wrong — click it:
lines: Magnets attract ferromagnetic metals — iron, nickel, cobalt and some alloys.
Copper, aluminium, gold and silver are not attracted: weakly diamagnetic or paramagnetic.
The fridge magnet ignores the aluminium can and grips the steel lid.
Stainless steel is always strongly magnetic, like any iron alloy.
The electron configuration decides — unpaired inner electrons plus the right lattice spacing.
config.correction: Stainless steel is often barely magnetic — its chromium and nickel content alter the lattice, which is why 'magnetic' is a terrible scrap-metal test for brass or anything else.
config.why: The electron configuration decides, not the label on the bin.

activities.anchor: acquire microscopic meaning in a solid
activities.caption: guess the magnitude — how fast do electrons actually drift?
activities.name: ssDriftEst

config.prompt: 1 A flows in 1 mm² copper wire (n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ carriers per m³, one free electron per atom). How fast do the electrons drift (v from I = nAqv)?
config.why: v ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁵ m/s — under a tenth of a millimetre per second. The light comes on instantly because the electric field establishes itself at near light speed, setting the whole wire's carriers drifting at once.
config.context: Enormous charge density, glacial drift speed, instant field — the correct replacement for the 'electrons whiz through wires' folk model.

activities.anchor: electrons carry the energy by travelling fast through the wire
activities.caption: true or false — the conveyor belt picture
activities.name: ssCargoJudge

statements.s: Electrons ferry the energy by racing along inside the wire.
statements.why: The drift speed is a slow crawl — the energy travels in the electromagnetic field around the wire, at close to light speed.

statements.s: The electrons are the conveyor belt, not the cargo.
statements.why: Which is why plumbing analogies and water in pipes eventually all fail as models.

statements.s: In an AC circuit the electrons simply oscillate in place, reversing direction 100 times a second at 50 Hz mains.
statements.why: Without ever completing a trip from socket to lamp.

statements.s: A perfect periodic lattice would resist electron flow like sand in a pipe.
statements.why: Quantum mechanics lets waves pass through perfect crystals unimpeded — resistance comes from imperfections.

activities.anchor: the study of how solids fail under electrical stress
activities.caption: walk the breakdown cascade
activities.name: ssBreakdownBranch

config.root: You crank the voltage across an insulator. Walk the failure.

start.text: Below the breakdown field, what do the insulator's electrons have?

choices.label: No accessible states — nothing to conduct with

wrong.text: Not yet — the avalanche is the failure mode, not the resting state.

climb.text: Force enough voltage across and electrons are torn free. What happens next?

choices.label: The freed electrons ionise more atoms — an avalanche multiplies them
The lattice quietly absorbs the stress

absorbed.text: Past the breakdown field there is no quiet absorption — the avalanche multiplies the freed electrons without limit.

flash.text: The solid becomes a conductor in a flash. Air sparks over at about 3 million volts per metre — which is why 11,000 V lines need their air gaps, and a wet finger is not a fly.

config.why: Every insulator has a breakdown field — 'insulator' means withstands, never impossible; the band gap delays conduction, it does not forbid it.

activities.caption: drag the divider — before and after the blue LED
activities.name: ssLedCompare

config.prompt: One device, two eras — drag to compare:

before.label: the historical problem
before.text: Red and green emitters existed (1.9 eV and 2.3 eV gaps), but the blue end stayed dark: the wide-gap crystals would not grow cleanly.

after.label: after the 1990s GaN breakthrough
after.text: Akasaki, Amano and Nakamura (Nobel 2014) grow gallium nitride cleanly — the primary colours complete, and white LEDs are blue emitters coated in a yellow phosphor. The same equation backwards runs solar cells and laser diodes.

config.why: λ = hc/E with the rule of thumb 1,240 nm per eV — a band gap chosen for its colour; 'band gap engineering' is a job title.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — past the breakdown field
activities.name: ssAirPredict

config.q: Air is an excellent insulator. You raise the voltage across a 1 mm gap past roughly 3 kV. What happens?
choices: Nothing — air never conducts, at any voltage
A tiny leakage current grows gradually with voltage
The air warms up but stays insulating
config.why: Past the breakdown field the conduction is catastrophic, not gradual — glass, rubber and plastics all have breakdown ratings, and every high-voltage design is a negotiation with them.

activities.anchor: find their deepest engineering expression in solids
activities.caption: pair each solid-state machine with its trick
activities.name: ssMachineMatch

config.prompt: Solids engineering their own electromagnetism — pair each with its trick:

pairs.right: a voltage appears across a current-carrying strip in a field — its sign revealed positive carriers, the holes of semiconductors
eddy currents in the pan's steel base — I²R heating with the hob's glass staying cool
domains that flip easily, low hysteresis loss — the transformer's choice
permanent magnets — the same phenomenon engineered in the opposite direction
chop the eddy-current loops that solid cores would offer

config.why: Hall sensors now measure position in every phone and car wheel — the same effect that settled a pre-quantum puzzle.
